<reason>Both sides ran a tight, well-structured clash on mechanism rather than the underlying duty, with strong pressure-question compliance on both sides. PRO's case was slightly more resilient across the exchange: it neutralized CON's "compliance theater/chilling effect" objection by noting that basic accessibility failures (unlabeled buttons, missing alt text, broken tab order) are publicly observable and don't require a confession or audit trail, and it exposed that CON's own alternatives (scorecards, procurement leverage) share the same detection/notice/bureaucracy burden CON attacked fines for, while lacking any price mechanism to move behavior. PRO also directly punctured CON's "drop the clinic vs. fine the platform" argument by noting that CON's own remediation-injunction alternative ("fix this or lose authorization") produces the same exit dynamic. CON's strongest late move—that a fine can simply be paid without guaranteeing a fix, whereas an injunction has a remedy path "built in"—is a genuinely sharp distinction and landed as the unanswered last word chronologically, but it doesn't fully escape PRO's "same exit" symmetry point, and CON's earlier answer to PRO's pressure question (citing lawsuits and procurement as existing non-fine costs) never engaged with PRO's specific rebuttal that lawsuits are "a lottery" and procurement rarely reaches non-government-adjacent organizations. That unaddressed gap weakens CON's response to the most direct pressure it faced. Overall PRO built a slightly more complete and internally consistent path to the motion.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's move that basic accessibility violations are publicly visible and don't require an audit "confession" to enforce (B4.3/B4.6) is the most decisive single rebuttal, since it directly dismantles CON's chilling-effect argument that fines would drive audits and honest disclosure underground.</best_rebuttal>
